content.content:
1	AMA Journal of Ethics®
2	May 2022, Volume 24, Number 5: E443-451
3	
4	VIEWPOINT: PEER-REVIEWED ARTICLE
5	Seven Points for Athletes to Consider Before Using a Dietary
6	Supplement
7	Amy B. Cadwallader, PhD
8	
9	         Abstract
10	         Performance-enhancing drugs (PEDs) have been used by athletes for as
11	         long as sporting competitions have existed. To protect the health and
12	         safety of athletes and promote fair play, banned substance lists were
13	         developed that include several classes of PEDs. Evidence shows that a
14	         majority of athletes use dietary supplement products to aid their training
15	         and support their health. Evidence also indicates that use of some
16	         dietary supplements carries a risk because the products may contain
17	         banned PEDs. Consumers and athletes should weigh a number of
18	         considerations before purchasing and consuming dietary supplements to
19	         protect their health, reputation, and the spirit of fair competition.
20	
21	The American Medical Association designates this journal-based CME activity for a maximum of 1 AMA PRA
22	Category 1 Credit™ available through the AMA Ed HubTM. Physicians should claim only the credit
23	commensurate with the extent of their participation in the activity.
24	
25	Why Performance-Enhancing Drug Use Matters
26	Performance-enhancing drugs (PEDs) have been used by athletes for decades, even
27	centuries. To promote fair play—an issue precipitated by the death of an athlete—the
28	International Olympic Committee (IOC) in 1967 banned the use of PEDs, established a
29	new Medical Commission, and created a list of banned substances.1 Mandatory testing
30	of all athletes began at the 1968 Olympic Games, and drug-testing programs were
31	initiated all over the world in the following years to further promote fair play and to
32	safeguard the health and safety of athletes.2
33	
34	In 1999, the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) was formed to promote and coordinate
35	the fight against doping in sport internationally. An IOC initiative, WADA was founded
36	with the support and participation of intergovernmental organizations, governments,
37	public authorities, and other public and private bodies fighting against doping in sports.3
38	
39	How a Substance Is Banned
40	WADA is considered the international standard and one of the most respected
41	organizations for identifying prohibited substances and methods. Each year, WADA
42	updates its Prohibited List to provide a comprehensive list of banned substances.4
43	WADA considers 3 criteria when reviewing substances for inclusion on the Prohibited
44	
45	
46	
47	
48	AMA Journal of Ethics, May 2022                                                                   443
49	 List, and any substance included on the list must fulfill at least 2 of the following
50	criteria5:
51	
52	      1. Substance has the potential to—or is proven to—enhance sport performance.
53	      2. Evidence exists of a potential or actual heath risk to an athlete.
54	      3. Use violates the spirit of sport as described in the World Anti-Doping Code.
55	
56	Classes of substances on banned substance lists include anabolic-androgenic steroids,
57	peptide hormones, growth factors, erythropoiesis stimulators, hormone modulators,
58	stimulants, diuretics, masking agents, and more.2 Although WADA sets the international
59	standard, each sport organization creates its own list based on the substances that put
60	athletes at risk or might be used to provide an unfair advantage. Banned substance lists
61	maintained by international, national, professional, amateur, and student sport
62	organizations are now commonplace and updated yearly. The consequences of athletes
63	being caught with a banned substance in their body include sanctions on eligibility for
64	athletic participation, reputational damage, and stripping of prizes and medals, in
65	addition to potential health risks or death.
66	
67	Associations Between Dietary Supplements and Banned Substances
68	Data indicate that between 40% and 70% of athletes use dietary supplements and that
69	between 10% and 15% of supplements may contain prohibited substances.6 While
70	many dietary supplement manufacturing companies make every effort to produce
71	quality products, it is well documented that unethical individuals and companies
72	continue to engage in the manufacturing and distribution of intentionally adulterated or
73	misbranded products labeled as dietary supplements.7,8,9,10,11 The most commonly
74	adulterated dietary supplements are those marketed as weight loss, sexual
75	enhancement, or sports supplements.9,10,12,13,14,15,16,17 From January 1, 2004 through
76	December 19, 2012, 51% of class I drug recalls in the United States were for dietary
77	supplements as opposed to pharmaceuticals,17 and copious reports detail the detection
78	of contaminants in dietary supplements.2,18,19,20,21
79	
80	Contamination of dietary supplements marketed to athletes is often due to
81	pharmaceutical adulteration, which occurs when an active pharmaceutical is included in
82	a product and not listed on the label.10 Pharmaceutical adulteration includes drugs
83	formerly approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and withdrawn, drugs
84	used in other countries and never FDA-approved experimental drugs that were minimally
85	or never tested in humans, veterinary drugs, and other novel compounds.22,23,24,25
86	Additionally, some compounds are intentionally designed and manufactured to avoid
87	regulations and evade standard detection and identification; most of these compounds
88	are added to dietary supplements without efficacy, safety, or toxicity assessments.26
89	
90	A former chair of the National Collegiate Athletic Association drug-testing committee
91	noted in an interview that most college students who report a positive drug test do so
92	because of substances, including steroids, found in over-the-counter dietary
93	supplements.27 However, when looking at shelves and aisles in stores and through
94	pages of products on the internet, how can consumers and athletes learn which ones
95	might contain banned substances or their markers?
96	
97	Seven Considerations
98	With this background in mind, the following considerations should be weighed by all
99	consumers and athletes before purchasing and consuming dietary supplements.
100	
101	
102	
103	
104	444                                                                    journalofethics.org
105	 Be educated about applicable banned substance lists. All athletes should know if there
106	is a banned substance list for their sporting organization and what substances are
107	included on it, as many ingredients in dietary supplements appear on banned substance
108	lists.2 Minimally, any athlete should have a trusted sports medical professional to
109	consult when thinking about using a dietary supplement.
110	
111	Be aware of strict liability and understand that athletes use any products at their own
112	risk. Most sports organizations hold athletes to a policy of strict liability, meaning that
113	athletes are solely responsible for the substances in their body, what they consume, and
114	for any subsequent consequences if metabolites or markers of banned substances are
115	found in a biofluid—regardless of whether they intentionally or inadvertently ingested a
116	prohibited substance (eg, in a contaminated dietary supplement).28 Regardless of intent,
117	athletes who take nutritional supplements risk damaging consequences.29 The provision
118	of strict liability is a common feature of the drug-testing programs of many sports
119	organizations.2
120	
121	Understand that supplement regulations differ from food and drug regulations.
122	Consumers, including athletes, often assume that dietary supplements are subject to
123	the same (or similar) regulations as over-the-counter or prescription medications; this is
124	not true. Dietary supplements are not reviewed premarket and are not held to the same
125	evidentiary standards of safety or efficacy as medications to be sold to consumers.
126	Medications go through a rigorous FDA approval process before entering the market;
127	drugs are considered unsafe until proven otherwise. Dietary supplements do not
128	undergo this approval process and are instead considered safe until contrary evidence
129	is provided. However, through the Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act of
130	1994, the FDA regulates the processing, manufacturing, labeling, and packaging of
131	dietary supplements.30 This act requires companies to ensure that their products are
132	safe and that the label claims are truthful and not misleading before they are brought to
133	market. The FDA is responsible for taking action against any adulterated or misbranded
134	dietary supplement product only after it reaches the market and a violation is found.31,32
135	
136	Always be skeptical—if a claim on a label sounds too good to be true, it probably is.
137	Claims such as Helps you use oxygen more efficiently, Make 10 lbs of muscle in a week,
138	Incinerate fat, and Get immediate results in energy, size, and strength are red flags.
139	Although a claim might sound enticing to athletes looking for a competitive edge,
140	extreme caution is warranted. Advertisement of awards won does not mean a product is
141	safe; in fact, such advertising might suggest a product contains a banned
142	substance.33,34
143	
144	Read the ingredients list and know what each ingredient is. Consumers, especially
145	athletes, should read the entire list of ingredients, understand what each ingredient is,
146	and be aware of the amount of each ingredient contained in a serving. New ingredients
147	continue to appear in products, yet few or no peer-reviewed publications assess
148	compounds’ pharmacology, toxicology, and safety. Compounds could be banned
149	substances or produce markers of banned substances.34,35 Some ingredients can cause
150	serious adverse events or be deadly.36,37,38,39
151	
152	Stimulants are a common contaminant in dietary supplements.11,40 The
153	bodybuilding.com 2012 supplement of the year was found to contain a
154	methamphetamine analog,34 and once including this particular drug in products fell out
155	of favor, another dangerous and banned stimulant became popular.41 Instances of
156	
157	
158	
159	
160	AMA Journal of Ethics, May 2022                                                        445
161	 contamination with prescription diuretics have also been documented,42,43,44 and
162	estrogenic compounds, anabolic agents—including anabolic‐androgenic steroids—are
163	frequently encountered in products marketed to athletes.45,46,47,48,49,50,51 Adulterants are
164	even found in dietary supplements for erectile dysfunction.19,52
165	
166	Look for third-party confirmation of the ingredients list from a trusted source. Often,
167	labels are intentionally confusing. Products have included false seals of approval noting
168	“banned substance free” while at the same time listing a substance banned by most
169	sport organizations among the ingredients. In light of such tactics, third-party
170	certification of product ingredients from a reputable and trusted source may be helpful.
171	With the large increase in dietary supplement manufacturers and the subsequent rise in
172	dietary supplement safety concerns, several companies have started independent
173	product certification services to provide an additional level of security and risk
174	minimization for consumers and athletes.53,54,55,56,57
175	
176	Unfortunately, it can often be a daunting challenge to collect and evaluate all the
177	information required to develop a strong sense of confidence in a supplement brand
178	and its products, which is a reason why third‐party certification is a desirable option for
179	supplement companies. Third‐party certification programs are designed to help protect
180	the rights and health of consumers and drug‐tested athletes by providing some
181	assurance that certified products are free of the prohibited substances for which they
182	are tested. No certification program can assure that a product is entirely free of
183	prohibited substances because it is not possible to test for all prohibited substances.
184	However, supplement companies that commit to third‐party certification have done
185	everything feasible to assure consumers that their certified products present minimal
186	risk of inadvertent doping. In addition to product certification, consumers can also
187	usually place trust in well-established companies with no previous issues with product
188	contamination, a good record with the FDA, and a commitment to scientific integrity
189	regarding claim substantiation.
190	
191	Additionally, understand what certification entails, as not all certifications are of equal
192	quality or content. Many companies test products to verify they contain the labeled
193	dose(s) of the active ingredient(s), while some companies test to confirm that products
194	do not contain microbes, heavy metals, or other toxins, and others test for a
195	comprehensive list of substances that are banned by athletic organizations.53,54,55,56,57
196	
197	Protect your health and reputation. Be sure to check with your physician or sports health
198	professional before consuming or incorporating any dietary supplement into your
199	routine. Do not take any supplement purchased from a store, online, or given to you by a
200	friend or relative without first discussing it with a medical professional who has your best
201	interests in mind.
202

AMA Journal of Ethics®
May 2022, Volume 24, Number 5: E443-451

VIEWPOINT: PEER-REVIEWED ARTICLE
Seven Points for Athletes to Consider Before Using a Dietary
Supplement
Amy B. Cadwallader, PhD

         Abstract
         Performance-enhancing drugs (PEDs) have been used by athletes for as
         long as sporting competitions have existed. To protect the health and
         safety of athletes and promote fair play, banned substance lists were
         developed that include several classes of PEDs. Evidence shows that a
         majority of athletes use dietary supplement products to aid their training
         and support their health. Evidence also indicates that use of some
         dietary supplements carries a risk because the products may contain
         banned PEDs. Consumers and athletes should weigh a number of
         considerations before purchasing and consuming dietary supplements to
         protect their health, reputation, and the spirit of fair competition.

The American Medical Association designates this journal-based CME activity for a maximum of 1 AMA PRA
Category 1 Credit™ available through the AMA Ed HubTM. Physicians should claim only the credit
commensurate with the extent of their participation in the activity.

Why Performance-Enhancing Drug Use Matters
Performance-enhancing drugs (PEDs) have been used by athletes for decades, even
centuries. To promote fair play—an issue precipitated by the death of an athlete—the
International Olympic Committee (IOC) in 1967 banned the use of PEDs, established a
new Medical Commission, and created a list of banned substances.1 Mandatory testing
of all athletes began at the 1968 Olympic Games, and drug-testing programs were
initiated all over the world in the following years to further promote fair play and to
safeguard the health and safety of athletes.2

In 1999, the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) was formed to promote and coordinate
the fight against doping in sport internationally. An IOC initiative, WADA was founded
with the support and participation of intergovernmental organizations, governments,
public authorities, and other public and private bodies fighting against doping in sports.3

How a Substance Is Banned
WADA is considered the international standard and one of the most respected
organizations for identifying prohibited substances and methods. Each year, WADA
updates its Prohibited List to provide a comprehensive list of banned substances.4
WADA considers 3 criteria when reviewing substances for inclusion on the Prohibited




AMA Journal of Ethics, May 2022                                                                   443
 List, and any substance included on the list must fulfill at least 2 of the following
criteria5:

      1. Substance has the potential to—or is proven to—enhance sport performance.
      2. Evidence exists of a potential or actual heath risk to an athlete.
      3. Use violates the spirit of sport as described in the World Anti-Doping Code.

Classes of substances on banned substance lists include anabolic-androgenic steroids,
peptide hormones, growth factors, erythropoiesis stimulators, hormone modulators,
stimulants, diuretics, masking agents, and more.2 Although WADA sets the international
standard, each sport organization creates its own list based on the substances that put
athletes at risk or might be used to provide an unfair advantage. Banned substance lists
maintained by international, national, professional, amateur, and student sport
organizations are now commonplace and updated yearly. The consequences of athletes
being caught with a banned substance in their body include sanctions on eligibility for
athletic participation, reputational damage, and stripping of prizes and medals, in
addition to potential health risks or death.

Associations Between Dietary Supplements and Banned Substances
Data indicate that between 40% and 70% of athletes use dietary supplements and that
between 10% and 15% of supplements may contain prohibited substances.6 While
many dietary supplement manufacturing companies make every effort to produce
quality products, it is well documented that unethical individuals and companies
continue to engage in the manufacturing and distribution of intentionally adulterated or
misbranded products labeled as dietary supplements.7,8,9,10,11 The most commonly
adulterated dietary supplements are those marketed as weight loss, sexual
enhancement, or sports supplements.9,10,12,13,14,15,16,17 From January 1, 2004 through
December 19, 2012, 51% of class I drug recalls in the United States were for dietary
supplements as opposed to pharmaceuticals,17 and copious reports detail the detection
of contaminants in dietary supplements.2,18,19,20,21

Contamination of dietary supplements marketed to athletes is often due to
pharmaceutical adulteration, which occurs when an active pharmaceutical is included in
a product and not listed on the label.10 Pharmaceutical adulteration includes drugs
formerly approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and withdrawn, drugs
used in other countries and never FDA-approved experimental drugs that were minimally
or never tested in humans, veterinary drugs, and other novel compounds.22,23,24,25
Additionally, some compounds are intentionally designed and manufactured to avoid
regulations and evade standard detection and identification; most of these compounds
are added to dietary supplements without efficacy, safety, or toxicity assessments.26

A former chair of the National Collegiate Athletic Association drug-testing committee
noted in an interview that most college students who report a positive drug test do so
because of substances, including steroids, found in over-the-counter dietary
supplements.27 However, when looking at shelves and aisles in stores and through
pages of products on the internet, how can consumers and athletes learn which ones
might contain banned substances or their markers?

Seven Considerations
With this background in mind, the following considerations should be weighed by all
consumers and athletes before purchasing and consuming dietary supplements.




444                                                                    journalofethics.org
 Be educated about applicable banned substance lists. All athletes should know if there
is a banned substance list for their sporting organization and what substances are
included on it, as many ingredients in dietary supplements appear on banned substance
lists.2 Minimally, any athlete should have a trusted sports medical professional to
consult when thinking about using a dietary supplement.

Be aware of strict liability and understand that athletes use any products at their own
risk. Most sports organizations hold athletes to a policy of strict liability, meaning that
athletes are solely responsible for the substances in their body, what they consume, and
for any subsequent consequences if metabolites or markers of banned substances are
found in a biofluid—regardless of whether they intentionally or inadvertently ingested a
prohibited substance (eg, in a contaminated dietary supplement).28 Regardless of intent,
athletes who take nutritional supplements risk damaging consequences.29 The provision
of strict liability is a common feature of the drug-testing programs of many sports
organizations.2

Understand that supplement regulations differ from food and drug regulations.
Consumers, including athletes, often assume that dietary supplements are subject to
the same (or similar) regulations as over-the-counter or prescription medications; this is
not true. Dietary supplements are not reviewed premarket and are not held to the same
evidentiary standards of safety or efficacy as medications to be sold to consumers.
Medications go through a rigorous FDA approval process before entering the market;
drugs are considered unsafe until proven otherwise. Dietary supplements do not
undergo this approval process and are instead considered safe until contrary evidence
is provided. However, through the Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act of
1994, the FDA regulates the processing, manufacturing, labeling, and packaging of
dietary supplements.30 This act requires companies to ensure that their products are
safe and that the label claims are truthful and not misleading before they are brought to
market. The FDA is responsible for taking action against any adulterated or misbranded
dietary supplement product only after it reaches the market and a violation is found.31,32

Always be skeptical—if a claim on a label sounds too good to be true, it probably is.
Claims such as Helps you use oxygen more efficiently, Make 10 lbs of muscle in a week,
Incinerate fat, and Get immediate results in energy, size, and strength are red flags.
Although a claim might sound enticing to athletes looking for a competitive edge,
extreme caution is warranted. Advertisement of awards won does not mean a product is
safe; in fact, such advertising might suggest a product contains a banned
substance.33,34

Read the ingredients list and know what each ingredient is. Consumers, especially
athletes, should read the entire list of ingredients, understand what each ingredient is,
and be aware of the amount of each ingredient contained in a serving. New ingredients
continue to appear in products, yet few or no peer-reviewed publications assess
compounds’ pharmacology, toxicology, and safety. Compounds could be banned
substances or produce markers of banned substances.34,35 Some ingredients can cause
serious adverse events or be deadly.36,37,38,39

Stimulants are a common contaminant in dietary supplements.11,40 The
bodybuilding.com 2012 supplement of the year was found to contain a
methamphetamine analog,34 and once including this particular drug in products fell out
of favor, another dangerous and banned stimulant became popular.41 Instances of




AMA Journal of Ethics, May 2022                                                        445
 contamination with prescription diuretics have also been documented,42,43,44 and
estrogenic compounds, anabolic agents—including anabolic‐androgenic steroids—are
frequently encountered in products marketed to athletes.45,46,47,48,49,50,51 Adulterants are
even found in dietary supplements for erectile dysfunction.19,52

Look for third-party confirmation of the ingredients list from a trusted source. Often,
labels are intentionally confusing. Products have included false seals of approval noting
“banned substance free” while at the same time listing a substance banned by most
sport organizations among the ingredients. In light of such tactics, third-party
certification of product ingredients from a reputable and trusted source may be helpful.
With the large increase in dietary supplement manufacturers and the subsequent rise in
dietary supplement safety concerns, several companies have started independent
product certification services to provide an additional level of security and risk
minimization for consumers and athletes.53,54,55,56,57

Unfortunately, it can often be a daunting challenge to collect and evaluate all the
information required to develop a strong sense of confidence in a supplement brand
and its products, which is a reason why third‐party certification is a desirable option for
supplement companies. Third‐party certification programs are designed to help protect
the rights and health of consumers and drug‐tested athletes by providing some
assurance that certified products are free of the prohibited substances for which they
are tested. No certification program can assure that a product is entirely free of
prohibited substances because it is not possible to test for all prohibited substances.
However, supplement companies that commit to third‐party certification have done
everything feasible to assure consumers that their certified products present minimal
risk of inadvertent doping. In addition to product certification, consumers can also
usually place trust in well-established companies with no previous issues with product
contamination, a good record with the FDA, and a commitment to scientific integrity
regarding claim substantiation.

Additionally, understand what certification entails, as not all certifications are of equal
quality or content. Many companies test products to verify they contain the labeled
dose(s) of the active ingredient(s), while some companies test to confirm that products
do not contain microbes, heavy metals, or other toxins, and others test for a
comprehensive list of substances that are banned by athletic organizations.53,54,55,56,57

Protect your health and reputation. Be sure to check with your physician or sports health
professional before consuming or incorporating any dietary supplement into your
routine. Do not take any supplement purchased from a store, online, or given to you by a
friend or relative without first discussing it with a medical professional who has your best
interests in mind.

       Short-Term D-Aspartic Acid Supplementation Does Not Affect
         Serum Biomarkers Associated With the Hypothalamic–
                 Pituitary–Gonadal Axis in Male Climbers
                           Blair Crewther, Konrad Witek, Piotr Zmijewski, and Zbigniew Obmiński
                                                       Institute of Sport—National Research Institute

     D-aspartic acid (DAA) is promoted as a testosterone (T) enhancing supplement by mechanisms involving the hypothalamic–
     pituitary–gonadal (HPG) axis. Here, we investigated the short-term effects of DAA on serum biomarkers of the HPG-axis in male
     climbers. Using a single-blinded, placebo-controlled design, 16 climbers were randomly assigned to either a DAA (3 g/day) or
     placebo (3 g/day) supplement for 2 weeks. The reverse treatment commenced after a 2-week washout, with all conditions
     administered in a balanced manner. The subjects maintained their normal weekly training across this study. Serum samples taken
     before and after each treatment were analyzed for T, luteinizing hormone, sex hormone binding globulin, and cortisol (C), and
     free T was calculated (cFT). The DAA supplement did not signiﬁcantly affect serum T, cFT, and luteinizing hormone levels.
     Only a main effect of time on sex hormone binding globulin (6.8% increase) and C (13.6% decrease) emerged (p < .03).
     Signiﬁcant negative associations were identiﬁed between pretest values and changes (%) in T, cFT, luteinizing hormone, and C
     levels with DAA and/or placebo, but these relationships did not differ between treatments (p > .46). Additional measures of
     physical function and serum hematology also failed to respond to DAA. In summary, a daily dose of DAA during a short training
     period did not inﬂuence T and selected indicators of the HPG-axis in male climbers. Other parameters linked to athletic
     performance and health status were also unaffected. Our ﬁndings support evidence showing that DAA (including DAA-blended
     supplements) at either recommended or higher dosages does not afford any ergogenic beneﬁts for athletic males.

  "abstract": "In a two-period crossover trial, 16 male climbers took 3 g/day of D-aspartic acid or placebo for two weeks. D-aspartic acid did not change serum testosterone, free testosterone or LH, and the only time effects were a rise in SHBG and a fall in cortisol.",
  "tldr": "In 16 male climbers, 3 g/day of D-aspartic acid for two weeks did not change testosterone, free testosterone or LH compared with placebo. Hormone findings in this small group do not support its use to raise testosterone in similar athletes.",

  "findings": "D-aspartic acid had no treatment or treatment-by-time effect on testosterone, free testosterone, LH, body mass or blood chemistry. Pre-treatment testosterone was negatively correlated with its change under placebo but not under DAA.",
  "limitations": "The abstract says physical function and haematology did not respond to DAA, but the results report a significant time effect on left-hand grip strength (+3.1%, p=.025), so the abstract overstates the null.   "rtp": "This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. Participants were healthy and injury-free, and no injured athletes or rehabilitation outcomes were studied."

                                                Practical HSR threshold deﬁnitions tailored to the capacities of each athlete
                                                are proposed, enabling a more evidence-based approach for the

{
 "id": "Q46",
 "sourceFile": "Should return to sport be delayed until 2 years after      ACL reconstruction - Biological and functional      considerations.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in text 'Should Return to Sport be Delayed Until 2 Years After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction? Biological and Functional Considerations' matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain": "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport",
 "domains": ["Rehabilitation & Return to Sport", "Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences": ["Rehabilitation", "Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Injured Athletes", "Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Narrative clinical review of biological (bone bruise, graft maturation, sensory), functional (neuromuscular control, quadriceps and hamstring strength, hop tests) and surgical/rehabilitation studies after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR), written as a Sports Medicine review article with no described search method. The authors argue that young, active athletes do not reach baseline joint health and function until about two years after ACLR, and that the second-injury risk is highest in the first two years, with nearly one in three of the younger cohort re-injured within that period.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The review uses no described search or selection method, so the evidence base cannot be checked for completeness. Its central recommendation, a two-year delay, is argued from mechanisms and cohort studies, and the review itself says no trial has tested it.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read a two-year minimum as an evidence-based rule for every athlete, when the paper argues for it as a postulate to be tested and does not give criteria for individual decisions.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2016,
  "citation": "Nagelli CV, Hewett TE. Should Return to Sport be Delayed Until 2 Years After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction? Biological and Functional Considerations. Sports Medicine. 2016.",
  "doi": "10.1007/s40279-016-0584-z",
  "abstract": "The authors argue that young, active athletes returning to high-level sport after ACL reconstruction have their highest second-injury risk in the first two years, and that the knee does not regain baseline biological and functional status until about two years. They conclude that delaying return to unrestricted sport to about two years would substantially reduce second ACL injuries.",
  "tldr": "Young, active athletes after ACL reconstruction carry their highest second-injury risk in the first two years, while bone, graft, proprioception and strength are still recovering. The authors propose a return-to-sport delay of about two years for high-risk athletes.",
  "methods": "This is a narrative review and opinion article (Sports Medicine) with no described search strategy or inclusion criteria. It draws on prospective and registry cohorts, imaging, proprioception, gait, hop-test and isokinetic strength studies after ACL reconstruction.",
  "findings": "Second ACL injury risk is highest in the first two years after ACLR in young, active athletes, and the authors cite a second-injury rate of nearly one in three in the younger cohort. Bone bruises, graft ligamentization and proprioceptive and strength deficits are reported to approach baseline around two years, although the review notes conflicting evidence on proprioception and bone bruise relevance.",
  "limitations": "The review has no described search method, so study selection cannot be reproduced. The two-year figure is an argued position, and the authors acknowledge that the relative contribution of sensory loss to second injury is unclear and that no trial has tested the delay. Much of the cited evidence comes from observational cohorts and small samples.",
  "practicalImplications": "Clinicians and staff can use the review to judge why early return may carry more risk for young athletes, and to weigh graft, bone and strength status in return-to-sport decisions. It does not establish a fixed two-year rule, and the authors frame it as a hypothesis to test.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance staff should note that the review's argument for delayed return is about joint health and second-injury risk, not performance. The review does not provide training or performance outcomes for athletes returning from ACLR.",
  "rtp": "The review directly addresses return to sport after ACLR, arguing for a delay of about two years for young, high-risk athletes. It should not be used to set a fixed date for an individual athlete, because it does not give validated readiness criteria or test the delay in a trial."
 }
}

8	Should We Lose Sleep Over Sleep
9	Disturbances After Sports-Related
10	Concussion? A Scoping Review of the
11	Literature
12	           David J. Stevens, PhD; Alia Alghwiri, PhD; Sarah L. Appleton, PhD; Jeffrey M. Rogers, PhD;
13	           Stephanie L. Plummer, PhD; Catharina Grant, PhD; Kelsey Bickley, BPsych (Hons);
14	           Pasquale K. Alvaro, PhD, MPsych (Clinical); Stephen Kennett, MBBS; Robert Adams, MD;
15	           Louis Holtzhausen, PhD, MBChB
16	
17	
18	             Objective: A single, severe traumatic brain injury can result in chronic sleep disturbances that can persist several years
19	             after the incident. In contrast, it is unclear whether there are sleep disturbances after a sports-related concussion
20	             (SRC). Considering growing evidence of links between sleep disturbance and neurodegeneration, this review
21	             examined the potential links between diagnosed SRCs and sleep disturbances to provide guidance for future
22	             studies. Methods: The scoping review undertook a systematic search of key online databases (Scopus, MEDLINE,
23	             SportDiscus, and Web of Science) using predetermined search terms for any articles that examined sleep after
24	             concussion. A screening criterion using agreed inclusion and exclusion criteria was utilized to ensure inclusion of
25	             relevant articles. Design: This scoping review is guided by the PRSIMA Scoping Review report. Results: Ten studies
26	             met the inclusion criteria, reporting on 896 adults who had experienced an SRC. Comparison with 1327 non-SRC
27	             adults occurred in 8 studies. Nine studies subjectively examined sleep, of which all but one study reported sleep
28	             disturbances after an SRC. Three studies objectively measured sleep, with 2 studies indicating large coefficients of
29	             variation of sleep duration, suggesting a range of sleep responses after an SRC. The only study to examine overnight
30	             polysomnography showed no differences in sleep metrics between those with and without an SRC. No studies
31	             examined interventions to improve sleep outcomes in people with concussion. Conclusions: This scoping review
32	             indicates preliminary evidence of sleep disturbances following an SRC. The heterogeneity of methodology used in
33	             the included studies makes consensus on the results difficult. Given the mediating role of sleep in neurodegenerative
34	             disorders, further research is needed to identify physiological correlates and pathological mechanisms of sleep
35	             disturbances in SRC-related neurodegeneration and whether interventions for sleep problems improve recovery
36	             from concussion and reduce the risk of SRC-related neurodegeneration. Key words: athletic injuries, brain concussion,
37	             craniocerebral trauma, chronic traumatic encephalopathy, sleep, sleep-wake disorders

Should We Lose Sleep Over Sleep
Disturbances After Sports-Related
Concussion? A Scoping Review of the
Literature
           David J. Stevens, PhD; Alia Alghwiri, PhD; Sarah L. Appleton, PhD; Jeffrey M. Rogers, PhD;
           Stephanie L. Plummer, PhD; Catharina Grant, PhD; Kelsey Bickley, BPsych (Hons);
           Pasquale K. Alvaro, PhD, MPsych (Clinical); Stephen Kennett, MBBS; Robert Adams, MD;
           Louis Holtzhausen, PhD, MBChB


             Objective: A single, severe traumatic brain injury can result in chronic sleep disturbances that can persist several years
             after the incident. In contrast, it is unclear whether there are sleep disturbances after a sports-related concussion
             (SRC). Considering growing evidence of links between sleep disturbance and neurodegeneration, this review
             examined the potential links between diagnosed SRCs and sleep disturbances to provide guidance for future
             studies. Methods: The scoping review undertook a systematic search of key online databases (Scopus, MEDLINE,
             SportDiscus, and Web of Science) using predetermined search terms for any articles that examined sleep after
             concussion. A screening criterion using agreed inclusion and exclusion criteria was utilized to ensure inclusion of
             relevant articles. Design: This scoping review is guided by the PRSIMA Scoping Review report. Results: Ten studies
             met the inclusion criteria, reporting on 896 adults who had experienced an SRC. Comparison with 1327 non-SRC
             adults occurred in 8 studies. Nine studies subjectively examined sleep, of which all but one study reported sleep
             disturbances after an SRC. Three studies objectively measured sleep, with 2 studies indicating large coefficients of
             variation of sleep duration, suggesting a range of sleep responses after an SRC. The only study to examine overnight
             polysomnography showed no differences in sleep metrics between those with and without an SRC. No studies
             examined interventions to improve sleep outcomes in people with concussion. Conclusions: This scoping review
             indicates preliminary evidence of sleep disturbances following an SRC. The heterogeneity of methodology used in
             the included studies makes consensus on the results difficult. Given the mediating role of sleep in neurodegenerative
             disorders, further research is needed to identify physiological correlates and pathological mechanisms of sleep
             disturbances in SRC-related neurodegeneration and whether interventions for sleep problems improve recovery
             from concussion and reduce the risk of SRC-related neurodegeneration. Key words: athletic injuries, brain concussion,
             craniocerebral trauma, chronic traumatic encephalopathy, sleep, sleep-wake disorders

 "id": "Q47",
 "sourceFile": "Should we lose sleep over sleep disturbances after sports-related concussion - A scoping review of the literature.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",

 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in text 'Should We Lose Sleep Over Sleep Disturbances After Sports-Related Concussion? A Scoping Review of the Literature' matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Brain Health & Psychology",
 "domains": ["Brain Health & Psychology", "Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Injured Athletes", "Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Scoping review (PRISMA-ScR) that searched Scopus, MEDLINE, SportDiscus and Web of Science for studies of sleep after sports-related concussion in adults. Ten studies were included, covering 896 concussed adults, with 1327 non-concussed adults in eight of them. Most subjective measures showed sleep disturbance after concussion, while the only polysomnography study found no differences from controls and the two actigraphy studies reported large variability in sleep duration.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The review did not assess risk of bias, and the included studies used varied concussion definitions, sleep measures and designs, with several using unvalidated single questions. Only one study used polysomnography, with 10 concussed and 11 control participants.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read this as evidence that concussion causes lasting sleep loss or raises neurodegeneration risk, but the paper reports only preliminary, mostly subjective associations and states that no clinical recommendations can yet be made.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2022,
  "citation": "Stevens DJ, et al. Should We Lose Sleep Over Sleep Disturbances After Sports-Related Concussion? A Scoping Review of the Literature. Journal of Head Trauma Rehabilitation. 2022;37(3):E206-E219.",
  "doi": "10.1097/HTR.0000000000000701",
  "abstract": "This scoping review searched four databases for studies of sleep after sports-related concussion in adults and included ten studies of 896 concussed adults. Most subjective measures found sleep disturbance after concussion, and the only polysomnography study found no differences from non-concussed controls.",
  "tldr": "Sleep disturbance is commonly reported after sports-related concussion in adults, but the evidence is preliminary and mostly subjective. The authors suggest asking about sleep in concussion assessments and screening for sleep disorders, while noting that intervention studies are lacking.",
  "methods": "Scoping review following PRISMA-ScR, with systematic searches of Scopus, MEDLINE, SportDiscus and Web of Science in November 2019 and September 2020. Included English-language cohort studies and RCTs of adults with athletic concussion that reported subjective or objective sleep outcomes, and ten studies were synthesised in a table without risk-of-bias ratings.",
  "findings": "Eight of nine studies that used subjective sleep measures reported some sleep disturbance after concussion. Two actigraphy studies found large coefficients of variation in sleep duration, and one study with 10 concussed and 11 control participants found no polysomnography differences despite worse self-rated sleep quality (PSQI 7.7 vs 3.5). Female athletes reported more sleep disturbance in one study, and no studies tested sleep interventions after concussion.",
  "limitations": "The authors note that the search was broad, which added methodological heterogeneity, and that the concussion and sleep measures were inconsistent. Several studies did not control for mental health problems or medication, and most sleep measures were subjective, with no objective data to corroborate them. The review covered only adults in sport, so findings may not transfer to children or to non-sport concussion.",
  "practicalImplications": "Staff can consider asking athletes about sleeping more or less than usual after a concussion, because current assessment tools miss hypersomnia. If sleep problems persist, the authors suggest a fuller sleep assessment with validated questionnaires or a sleep diary, and a referral to a sleep specialist when symptoms persist.",
  "athleteDev": "This review is about concussion recovery and brain health, not training or performance. It does not show how sleep after concussion affects performance, so it cannot guide performance or workload decisions.",
  "rtp": "The review can inform return-to-sport screening by showing that sleep disturbance is often reported after concussion and that current tools may miss some of it. It cannot set a sleep-based criterion for return to play, because no studies tested whether treating sleep changes recovery."
 }
}

  "athleteDev": "Performance staff should note that the review's argument for delayed return is about joint health and second-injury risk, not performance. The review does not provide training or performance outcomes for athletes returning from ACLR.",
